sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You'll learn how to turn the best prompts you've written into reusable templates — and how to build a personal prompt library that grows with you throughout this course and beyond.

## The Problem With Starting From Scratch

Every time you sit down with an AI tool and type a prompt from scratch, you're leaving efficiency on the table. You've already figured out what works for your recurring tasks — your prompts for email replies, meeting summaries, code reviews, status updates. Writing them fresh each time wastes time and produces inconsistent results.

The solution is a prompt library: a collection of your best prompts, formatted as templates with variable slots, stored somewhere you can access instantly.

This is the prompting equivalent of keyboard shortcuts. The first time you invest a few minutes setting one up, you save that time on every future use. A good prompt library built during this course will save you hours every month for years.

**The shift in mindset:** Stop thinking of prompts as throwaway text you type once. Start thinking of them as tools you build once and reach for repeatedly.

## Template Syntax: Using [BRACKETS] for Variables

The simplest way to make a prompt reusable is to replace the parts that change with bracketed placeholders. The convention is `[VARIABLE_NAME]` in uppercase — it's immediately visible and easy to find-and-replace.

Here's a prompt you might write once:

"Write a polite follow-up email to Marcus at Acme Corp about the proposal I sent on May 5th, reminding him that the deadline is May 20th."

Turned into a reusable template:

Write a polite follow-up email to [RECIPIENT_NAME] at [COMPANY] about
[TOPIC]. I sent my initial message on [DATE_SENT]. The deadline or next
step is [DEADLINE_OR_NEXT_STEP].

Keep the tone friendly but direct. Three paragraphs maximum. Do not use
phrases like 'I hope this email finds you well.'

Now you have a template you fill in for any follow-up email. The constraint at the bottom (no clichés) is pre-baked because you already know you don't want that.

Let's look at more examples.

Summarise this meeting in the following format:

**Meeting:** [MEETING_NAME]
**Date:** [DATE]
**Attendees:** [NAMES]

**Key Decisions Made:**
[bullet list]

**Action Items:**
[Name — Task — Due Date]

**Open Questions / Parking Lot:**
[bullet list]

Meeting notes to summarise:
[PASTE NOTES HERE]

Act as a senior [LANGUAGE] developer doing a thorough code review.

Review this code for:
1. Correctness — does it do what it's supposed to do?
2. Edge cases — what inputs could break it?
3. Readability — would a junior developer understand it?
4. Anything that would fail a PR review at a professional company

Be specific about line numbers or sections. Don't be diplomatic.

Code:
[PASTE CODE HERE]

Write a concise weekly status update for my [ROLE] role at [COMPANY].

Audience: my manager and the team.
Tone: professional and direct — no fluff.

Use this structure:
**This week:** [3 bullet points of what I accomplished]
**Next week:** [3 bullet points of what I'm working on]
**Blockers:** [Any issues I need help with, or 'None']

My notes for this week:
[PASTE YOUR RAW NOTES OR BULLET POINTS HERE]

Teach me [TOPIC] as if I'm a smart adult with no prior knowledge of it.

Structure your explanation as:
1. The core idea in one sentence
2. Why it matters (a real-world consequence of not understanding it)
3. How it works — use an analogy from [ANALOGY_DOMAIN, e.g. 'cooking', 'sport', 'construction']
4. One concrete example
5. The one thing I should learn next

No jargon. If you use a technical term, define it immediately.

**Build the constraints into the template.** Every time you refine a prompt — removing a cliché, capping the length, adding a specific format — bake that refinement into the template. The template should reflect your fully-learned preferences, not your first attempt.

## Where to Store Your Prompt Library

You have several good options. Pick the one you'll actually use:

**VS Code snippet file** — Create a markdown file in your project's `prompts/` folder. This is searchable and lives with your code. If you use VS Code daily, this is the most accessible option.

**Text expansion tool** — Apps like AutoHotkey (Windows) or Espanso let you type a short abbreviation (e.g. `;;email`) and it expands to your full template. The fastest option if you run prompts frequently.

**Claude Project Instructions** — Paste your most-used templates into the instructions of a Claude Project. They're there every time you open that project without copy-pasting.

**Notion or Google Docs** — A simple table: Template Name | Category | Template Text | Notes. Easy to search and share with a team.

The format matters less than the habit. The habit is: **every time a prompt works well, save it before you close the tab.**

**The Anthropic Prompt Library** at anthropic.com/research/prompt-library is an excellent source of starting templates. The community resource Awesome ChatGPT Prompts (github.com/f/awesome-chatgpt-prompts) has hundreds more. Neither replaces your personal library — they're raw material you'll adapt to your real needs.

sections.title: Build Your Prompt Library
sections.content:
This workshop is different from the others in Part 3 — it's a documentation and organisation task, not a browser session. You're building something that will save you time every week from here on.

**Step 1 — Create the file**

Open VS Code (or Notepad if VS Code isn't installed yet) and create a file called `prompts/my-prompt-library.md`.

**Step 2 — Add your Part 3 prompts**

Go back through lessons 3-1 through 3-7. Find every prompt you wrote or saved during those workshops. Add the best ones to your library using this format for each:

```
## [Category / Use Case Name]

[The template text with [VARIABLE] placeholders]

**Example (filled in):**
[One filled-in example showing the template in use]

**Notes:**
[Any constraints, context, or tips for using this template]
```

**Step 3 — Add 3 new templates**

Now think about your own recurring tasks — things you do at work, at home, or in your learning. Write 3 prompt templates for tasks specific to your life:

- What do you write repeatedly? (emails, reports, messages)
- What do you research repeatedly? (prices, products, topics)
- What do you analyse repeatedly? (decisions, documents, data)

For each one, write the template with `[VARIABLE]` placeholders and one filled-in example.

**Step 4 — Save and commit**

Save the file. If you've set up Git (from Part 5), commit it: `git commit -m "Add prompt library"`

This file will grow throughout the course. Treat it as a living document — add to it whenever you find a prompt that works.

**You've completed Part 3 — Prompt Engineering.** You now have a systematic toolkit: the four-element framework, role prompting, chain-of-thought, few-shot examples, structured output, iterative refinement, and a personal prompt library. These are the skills that separate people who get mediocre AI output from people who get excellent AI output — consistently.
